_meta.question: What should store Jod's state on a single VPS, given many agent processes read and write it concurrently?
_meta.note: Every record carries a `lesson` — the one idea worth stealing even if the option loses. That field is the point of the survey, not the ranking.

candidates.name: Flat markdown + JSONL (status quo)
candidates.concurrency: append-only is atomic under O_APPEND for <PIPE_BUF writes; anything else races
candidates.status_2026: Jod's current plan: OKF notes + ~/.jod/runs/*/stream.jsonl.
disqualifiers: no atomic read-modify-write
no secondary index
no vector recall
rescan cost grows linearly
candidates.lesson: Plain files at the boundary is a real feature: greppable, diffable, survives the process dying, and needs no daemon. Keep files as the interchange format even after the index moves into a database.

candidates.name: SQLite (WAL) + FTS5 + sqlite-vec
candidates.concurrency: WAL: readers never block the writer; exactly one writer at a time, others get SQLITE_BUSY and must retry
candidates.graph: recursive CTE, or GraphQLite extension for openCypher
candidates.status_2026: sqlite-vec is the surviving embedded vector extension; sqlite-vss is deprecated.
candidates.lesson: One file, zero daemons, and the writer bottleneck is only a bottleneck if write transactions are long. Short append transactions serialize at a rate far above what agents generate.

candidates.name: SQLite BEGIN CONCURRENT (wal2 branch)
candidates.concurrency: multiple write txns proceed in parallel, COMMIT still serialized; conflict = page overlap, retry required
candidates.status_2026: Still never merged to mainline SQLite. Lives on in forks (libSQL, Turso).
disqualifiers: not in mainline; you ship a custom SQLite build forever
candidates.lesson: Page-level optimistic conflict is the wrong granularity for hot append tables — every writer touches the same rightmost btree page, so they all conflict. Row-level MVCC is what actually helps appends.

candidates.name: SQLite HC-tree backend
candidates.concurrency: experimental high-concurrency backend, row-level conflict detection
candidates.status_2026: Long-running SQLite experiment, no release date, storage format unstable.
disqualifiers: experimental
no stable on-disk format
candidates.lesson: Proof that the SQLite team agrees the single-writer limit is worth fixing — and that fixing it means replacing the storage engine, not tuning locks.

candidates.name: libSQL (Turso's C fork of SQLite)
candidates.concurrency: SQLite semantics, plus a server mode (sqld) and embedded replicas with write-through
candidates.status_2026: Production engine behind Turso Cloud. Turso is steering toward the Rust rewrite long-term.
candidates.lesson: Server mode over one SQLite file is the cheapest way to get real multi-process writes: one process owns the file, everyone else speaks a protocol. The bottleneck moves from lock contention to IPC.

candidates.name: Turso Database (SQLite rewritten in Rust, ex-Limbo)
candidates.concurrency: BEGIN CONCURRENT over an MVCC engine; row-granular conflict detection at commit
candidates.status_2026: Concurrent writes shipped as early preview on Turso Cloud 2026-08-03. Engine still beta; also speaks Postgres wire experimentally.
disqualifiers: beta
on-disk/feature surface still moving
candidates.lesson: The most direct answer to the exact question asked — SQLite ergonomics with row-level MVCC. Worth tracking closely; too young to bet an unattended agent's memory on today.

candidates.name: DuckDB (+ VSS)
candidates.concurrency: many readers OR one writing process; a second process cannot even open the file read-write
candidates.status_2026: v1.5.x. Multi-writer answers are DuckLake (catalog in Postgres) and the Quack client/server protocol (beta, targeting v2.0 in autumn 2026).
disqualifiers: one writing process, full stop — a hard blocker for multi-agent writes
candidates.lesson: Unbeatable for the analytics half (scan the whole event log, aggregate spend). Read-only attach to a file another engine owns is the right way to use it — as a query engine, not a store of record.

candidates.name: DuckLake (DuckDB + Postgres catalog)
candidates.concurrency: concurrent writers coordinate through a transactional SQL catalog; data in Parquet
candidates.status_2026: v1.0 spec + implementation published April 2026, declared production-intended.
disqualifiers: you already need Postgres for the catalog, so Postgres alone is simpler
per-commit overhead is far too high for per-event appends
candidates.lesson: The lakehouse insight: put the *catalog* in a transactional store and the *data* in immutable files. That is exactly the shape of 'markdown files + an index database' — validation of the hybrid, not a replacement for it.

candidates.name: PGlite (Postgres compiled to WASM)
candidates.concurrency: one process, single connection
candidates.status_2026: Popular for browser/local-first apps and test harnesses.
disqualifiers: single process — fails the core requirement outright
candidates.lesson: Postgres semantics with no daemon is possible, and it makes 'develop against the same engine you deploy' cheap. Useful as a test fixture for a Postgres-based design.

candidates.name: SurrealDB
candidates.concurrency: delegates concurrency control to the storage backend (RocksDB / SurrealKV / TiKV)
candidates.status_2026: Actively developed, markets itself for agent context.
disqualifiers: BSL licence
one engine covering relational+graph+vector+FTS means none of them is best-in-class
smaller operational track record
candidates.lesson: The multi-model pitch is genuinely attractive for agent memory, where one fact wants to be a row, a node and a vector at once. The cost is betting everything on one young engine.

candidates.name: Kùzu (embedded property graph)
candidates.concurrency: one writer process
candidates.status_2026: Acquired by Apple in October 2025; open-source repository archived. On-disk format never stabilised.
disqualifiers: ARCHIVED — no upstream
unstable storage format required export/reimport across versions
candidates.lesson: A cautionary tale that outranks its technical merits: the embedded-graph niche is thin enough that its best project got absorbed. Weight project survival as heavily as benchmarks.

candidates.name: CozoDB (Datalog + vector + graph, embedded)
candidates.concurrency: MVCC via RocksDB
candidates.status_2026: Development has largely stalled.
disqualifiers: dormant upstream
candidates.lesson: Datalog is the most natural query language for 'what do I know about X, transitively' — the actual shape of agent recall. Nobody has shipped it in a maintained embedded engine yet.

candidates.name: GraphQLite (SQLite extension, openCypher)
candidates.concurrency: SQLite WAL semantics
candidates.graph: property graph + openCypher over SQLite tables
candidates.status_2026: Jod's currently-planned pillar 2 driver.
disqualifiers: young, small community
candidates.lesson: Graph as an extension over SQLite means the graph, the events and the vectors share one file and one transaction. That co-location is worth more than a faster standalone graph engine.

candidates.name: redb / sled / fjall / RocksDB (+ usearch)
candidates.concurrency: one write txn at a time, lock-free readers
candidates.status_2026: Stable building blocks; redb and fjall are the maintained modern Rust choices.
disqualifiers: you are writing a database, not using one
no query language, no ad-hoc inspection by an agent
candidates.lesson: Rejecting this defines a real requirement: an agent must be able to explore its own memory with an ad-hoc query it composes at runtime. That demands SQL or Cypher, not a get/put API.

candidates.name: LMDB
candidates.concurrency: genuinely multi-process: readers are lock-free via mmap, one writer via a file lock
candidates.status_2026: Unchanged and unkillable.
disqualifiers: key-value only
candidates.lesson: The cleanest existence proof that multi-process embedded concurrency is a solved problem when reads are mmap'd snapshots and writes are serialized. This is the same bet SQLite WAL makes.

candidates.name: LanceDB (Lance columnar format)
candidates.concurrency: each write creates a new table version; concurrent committers retry a bounded number of times then fail
candidates.status_2026: The default embedded vector store; multi-writer works but is documented as retry-bounded.
disqualifiers: commit contention under many small writers
no relational joins or constraints
candidates.lesson: Versioned tables give you time-travel over agent memory for free — 'what did I believe last Tuesday' is a table version, not a schema you designed. Best-in-class at larger-than-memory vector scans.

candidates.name: Chroma
candidates.concurrency: embedded mode is one process; server mode serializes
candidates.status_2026: Rewritten core in Rust; still positioned for prototyping.
disqualifiers: thin layer over SQLite+HNSW — inherits SQLite's limits without SQLite's guarantees
candidates.lesson: The ergonomics are the product: `add(documents=[...])` with embeddings handled for you. Whatever wins should hide embedding plumbing that well.

candidates.name: Milvus Lite / Milvus standalone
candidates.concurrency: standalone is many-writer via a message queue; Lite is single-process
candidates.status_2026: The scale leader; standalone still pulls etcd + object storage.
disqualifiers: footprint is absurd for one VPS
no transactional state store
candidates.lesson: Separating write path (log) from index build (background compaction) is why it absorbs write bursts. Any design that indexes synchronously on the write path will stall agents.

candidates.name: FAISS / hnswlib / usearch / Annoy
candidates.concurrency: no cross-process story; persistence is save/load of the whole index
candidates.vector: the state of the art in ANN itself
candidates.status_2026: usearch is the modern pick; FAISS remains the research baseline.
disqualifiers: not a database — no durability, no concurrency, no filtering
candidates.lesson: Every vector database on this list is one of these plus a storage engine. Which means the vector index is the *easy* part, and the concurrency and durability story is what you are actually shopping for.

candidates.name: Qdrant
candidates.concurrency: high concurrent write + search; optimistic segment updates
candidates.vector: native HNSW + quantization + rich payload filtering
candidates.fulltext: payload text match, not real BM25
candidates.status_2026: The strongest single-node dedicated vector server; best filtered-search story.
disqualifiers: a second system to run and back up
no transactional state store, so you still need SQLite/Postgres beside it
candidates.lesson: Best-in-class *filtered* vector search — pre-filtering by payload without wrecking recall is the hard part, and Qdrant solved it. If recall-under-filter ever becomes the bottleneck, this is the escape hatch.

candidates.name: Weaviate
candidates.concurrency: good
candidates.status_2026: Mature, module ecosystem, JVM-scale memory appetite.
disqualifiers: heavy for one small VPS
candidates.lesson: Hybrid search (BM25 + vector, fused) is not a nice-to-have for agent recall — exact identifiers like error codes and file paths are why pure vector recall disappoints.

candidates.name: Typesense / Meilisearch
candidates.concurrency: write batching, near-real-time index
candidates.status_2026: Strong keyword search, vector as a companion feature.
disqualifiers: not a store of record
candidates.lesson: Typo tolerance and prefix search matter when the query is generated by a model that half-remembers a name. Pure embedding recall handles fuzziness differently and misses exact-ish matches.

candidates.name: Elasticsearch / OpenSearch
candidates.concurrency: excellent, but eventually visible
candidates.status_2026: Still the hybrid-search benchmark; still a JVM.
disqualifiers: JVM footprint eats a small VPS
refresh-interval means writes are not immediately readable — poison for read-your-own-write agent state
candidates.lesson: Near-real-time indexing is a trap for agent state. An agent that writes a fact and immediately re-reads it must see it; search engines deliberately do not promise that.

candidates.name: PostgreSQL 18 + pgvector
candidates.concurrency: many concurrent writers, no global write lock; the reference answer for this workload
candidates.fulltext: tsvector/GIN, or ParadeDB pg_search for real BM25
candidates.txn: full ACID, snapshot isolation, advisory locks, SKIP LOCKED
candidates.status_2026: pgvector/pgvector:pg18 image; consensus is Postgres-resident vectors are right up to low tens of millions.
disqualifiers: a daemon to run, tune and back up
not greppable when the daemon is down
candidates.lesson: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is a work queue, LISTEN/NOTIFY is an event bus, and pgvector is recall — one process replaces three. That consolidation, not raw speed, is the argument.

candidates.name: pgvectorscale (StreamingDiskANN)
candidates.concurrency: inherits Postgres
candidates.vector: disk-oriented DiskANN index, label-aware filtering, SBQ compression
candidates.status_2026: The scaling path when the HNSW index no longer fits in RAM.
disqualifiers: extra extension to build/install
candidates.lesson: The failure mode of vector search on a small VPS is the index not fitting in RAM, not the algorithm being slow. A disk-first index is the fix, and it is a drop-in upgrade rather than a migration.

candidates.name: ParadeDB (pg_search / pg_analytics)
candidates.concurrency: inherits Postgres
candidates.fulltext: real BM25 via Tantivy, inside Postgres
candidates.status_2026: The strongest option for hybrid BM25+vector in one SQL query.
disqualifiers: AGPL
another extension in the image
candidates.lesson: Hybrid ranking belongs in the same query as the filter and the join. Fusing results in application code means you cannot ORDER BY the fused score and LIMIT correctly.

candidates.name: Apache AGE (openCypher in Postgres)
candidates.concurrency: inherits Postgres
candidates.status_2026: Version lag behind mainline Postgres is the usual complaint.
disqualifiers: tracks Postgres releases slowly
traversal perf well behind native graph engines
candidates.lesson: If the graph is small — thousands of notes, not billions of edges — a recursive CTE beats installing a graph engine. Reach for Cypher when the queries get hard to write, not when the data gets big.

candidates.name: MySQL 9 / MariaDB 11.8 (native VECTOR)
candidates.concurrency: good
candidates.status_2026: Vector support landed; ecosystem for AI work is far behind Postgres.
disqualifiers: no reason to pick it over Postgres here
candidates.lesson: Nothing Postgres does not do better for this workload. Included so the survey is honest about having considered it.

candidates.name: MongoDB / FerretDB
candidates.concurrency: good, document-level
candidates.vector: Atlas Vector Search (managed only for the good version)
candidates.status_2026: Vector search is strongest on Atlas, weakest self-hosted.
disqualifiers: self-hosted vector story is poor
SSPL
candidates.lesson: Schemaless suits agent memory better than it gets credit for — an agent inventing a new fact shape should not need a migration. JSONB in Postgres captures most of that benefit.

candidates.name: ClickHouse
candidates.concurrency: excellent for batched appends, poor for row updates
candidates.vector: approximate index (newer), brute force is genuinely fast
candidates.status_2026: Increasingly pitched for observability of agent traces.
disqualifiers: no transactions, no row updates — wrong for mutable agent state
candidates.lesson: The right home for the *transcript* if event volume ever explodes. Agent traces are observability data, and observability data belongs in a columnar store, not beside your state.

candidates.name: TiDB / CockroachDB / YugabyteDB
candidates.concurrency: excellent, horizontally scalable
candidates.vector: TiDB has native vector; Cockroach added it
candidates.status_2026: Frequently recommended for multi-agent workloads by vendors.
disqualifiers: a cluster on a single 4-core VPS is strictly worse than one Postgres
Raft round-trips add latency you gain nothing for
candidates.lesson: The vendor advice to reach for distributed SQL answers a scaling question nobody with one VPS has. Distribution is a cost you pay for availability, not a performance feature.

candidates.name: Redis 8 (vector sets) / Valkey + valkey-search
candidates.concurrency: atomic commands, no lock contention by construction; sub-ms
candidates.vector: vector sets (HNSW) in Redis 8; valkey-search module for Valkey
candidates.status_2026: Redis 8.x has native vector sets; Valkey 8.1 is ~8% faster, 20% less memory, BSD.
disqualifiers: durability is a tradeoff dial (AOF fsync), not a guarantee
dataset must fit in RAM
Redis licence pushed the community to Valkey
candidates.lesson: Single-threaded command execution means read-modify-write is atomic for free — no BUSY, no retry, no deadlock. Streams also make it the best pure A2A message bus on this list.

candidates.name: NATS JetStream (streams + KV)
candidates.concurrency: excellent multi-producer; KV has compare-and-swap
candidates.status_2026: The lightweight broker of choice; single static binary.
disqualifiers: no query capability at all — you cannot ask it a question
candidates.lesson: Exactly right for the A2A inbox/outbox half of Jod, and it replaces tailing JSONL with real delivery semantics (durable consumers, replay, acks). Complements a database rather than competing with one.

candidates.name: Kafka / Redpanda
candidates.concurrency: the reference multi-producer design
candidates.status_2026: Redpanda removes the JVM but not the operational weight.
disqualifiers: enormous overkill for a handful of agents on one box
candidates.lesson: Partition-per-key is how you get ordered, parallel writes without locks. The same trick works in miniature: one append target per agent, merged on read.

candidates.name: Neo4j / Memgraph / FalkorDB
candidates.concurrency: good
candidates.vector: Neo4j and FalkorDB both have vector indexes
candidates.status_2026: FalkorDB (Redis-module lineage) is the lightweight option; Neo4j is the JVM heavyweight.
disqualifiers: footprint and licence
a dedicated graph server for a few thousand notes is unjustifiable
candidates.lesson: Graph engines earn their keep on variable-length traversals over millions of edges. Jod's brain is thousands of notes — the graph is a query pattern here, not a scale problem.

candidates.name: Dolt (Git-for-data, MySQL-compatible)
candidates.concurrency: agents write isolated branches; conflicts surface at merge, not at write time
candidates.status_2026: Explicitly repositioned in 2025-2026 as 'the database for AI agents' — branch per agent, review the diff, merge or roll back.
disqualifiers: no vector search
write throughput well below Postgres
merge conflicts become a workflow you must staff
candidates.lesson: The single most interesting idea in the whole survey: an agent's writes should be *proposals*, not facts. Jod already does this for code via git worktrees — the same discipline applied to data is a real answer to 'what if an agent corrupts my memory'.

candidates.name: XTDB / Datomic (bitemporal, immutable)
candidates.concurrency: readers are lock-free over immutable snapshots; one transactor serializes writes
candidates.status_2026: XTDB v2 speaks the Postgres wire protocol, which makes it far more approachable.
disqualifiers: single transactor caps write throughput
small ecosystem
JVM
candidates.lesson: Bitemporality is the correct model for agent memory and almost nobody implements it: you need both 'when was this true' and 'when did I learn it'. Contradiction resolution is impossible without that second axis — retrofit it as two timestamp columns.

candidates.name: TerminusDB
candidates.concurrency: commit-based
candidates.rust_client: core is Rust, client is HTTP
candidates.status_2026: Niche, slow-moving.
disqualifiers: small community
unusual data model to learn
candidates.lesson: Same branch/merge idea as Dolt but on a graph. Reinforces that versioning and knowledge graphs compose well — a note's edit history is itself a useful thing to query.

candidates.name: ElectricSQL / Zero / PowerSync
candidates.concurrency: local writes, async replication, server-authoritative resolution
candidates.status_2026: Mature local-first sync over Postgres.
disqualifiers: solves a distribution problem Jod does not have on one VPS
candidates.lesson: Directly relevant to Jod's actual roadmap: laptop + VPS + a planned iOS client all wanting the same brain. Note that these all chose Postgres as the authoritative upstream — that is a meaningful vote.

candidates.name: Automerge / Yjs (CRDTs)
candidates.concurrency: unlimited concurrent writers by construction
candidates.status_2026: The local-first standard for collaborative documents.
disqualifiers: convergence is not correctness — two agents 'both win' on a counter or a task claim, which is exactly wrong for task assignment
no queries
candidates.lesson: Sharpens the requirement: some agent state genuinely needs a *winner* (who owns this task), and CRDTs structurally refuse to pick one. Use them for prose notes, never for coordination.

candidates.name: FoundationDB
candidates.concurrency: the strongest correctness story in the industry
candidates.status_2026: Still the substrate other databases are built on.
disqualifiers: a layer-building exercise, not a database you use
5-second transaction limit
cluster overhead
candidates.lesson: Its deterministic simulation testing is why it is trusted. The transferable idea: test the concurrency story by simulating adversarial interleavings, not by hoping.

candidates.name: Managed Postgres (RDS / Aurora / Neon / Supabase / Timescale)
candidates.concurrency: same as Postgres, plus HA and PITR
candidates.status_2026: Neon offers instant branching; Supabase bundles auth/storage/realtime.
disqualifiers: network RTT on every query from the VPS
violates Jod's local-first rule — Jod stops working when the network does
ongoing cost
candidates.lesson: Neon's database branching is Dolt's idea with Postgres compatibility, and it is the least-friction way to get 'give each agent an isolated copy'. If the local-first rule were ever relaxed, this is where it would go.

candidates.name: Turso Cloud (managed libSQL)
candidates.concurrency: embedded replicas give zero-latency local reads with write-through
candidates.status_2026: Concurrent writes in early preview since 2026-08-03; database-per-tenant is cheap.
disqualifiers: cloud dependency for writes
candidates.lesson: Embedded replica is the best-shaped idea for a laptop+VPS setup: reads never leave the process, writes go to one authority. It is CQRS with the complexity hidden.

candidates.name: Mem0
candidates.concurrency: inherits backends
candidates.status_2026: Dual-store: vectors for semantics, graph for relationships. LLM call on the write path to extract facts.
disqualifiers: not a database — it is a policy layer, and it still needs you to choose the database underneath
an LLM call per write is slow and non-deterministic
candidates.lesson: The separation worth stealing: *what to remember* is a policy question, *where to put it* is a storage question. Do not let a framework answer the second by accident.

candidates.name: Zep / Graphiti (temporal knowledge graph)
candidates.concurrency: inherits backends; LLM extraction is the real bottleneck
candidates.graph: temporal knowledge graph — every edge carries valid-from/valid-to
candidates.status_2026: Graph-first agent memory; reports beating Mem0 by ~15 points on LongMemEval.
disqualifiers: Python service in a Rust system
LLM extraction cost per write
was leaning on Kuzu, which is now archived
candidates.lesson: Model fact *invalidation* explicitly: when a new fact contradicts an old one, mark the old edge invalid rather than deleting it. This is the single highest-value schema idea in the survey and costs two columns.

candidates.name: Letta (MemGPT)
candidates.concurrency: inherits Postgres
candidates.status_2026: Agent-as-a-service with self-editing memory blocks; standardised on Postgres.
disqualifiers: owns the agent loop — conflicts directly with Jod's 'harnesses think, Jod delegates' rule
candidates.lesson: Its tiered split (small always-in-context core block + large searchable archive) is the right memory shape, and it is a schema decision, not a product you must buy. Also: it chose Postgres.
